claims_disputed.claim: Wave dispatch approaches the critical-path bound (CP ratio 1.03-1.11, up to 14.3x speedup) and gives ~1.4x on a 2-slot local backend.
claims_disputed.reason: The CP ratio applies to sleep tasks, where any level-synchronous topological scheduler would trivially do this, and all three baselines 'serialize execution' (§6.3). On the real backend, the abstract and contributions say 1.4x 'matches the hardware concurrency ceiling', but §6.3 says a perfect 2-slot dispatcher would deliver 2.0x. The reported variant is also capped to the slot count, because the uncapped wave dispatcher 'regresses bimodally'. So the paper's own scheduler underperforms the ceiling it claims to match.

claims_disputed.claim: Human review reduces residual defects 0.47->0.03 per task.
claims_disputed.reason: The 0.47 Auto-SPOQ baseline (Table 10) is worse than the No-Validation mode in Table 8 (0.34), on what §6.2 says are the same four tasks, model and environment. With a baseline that anomalous, the delta cannot be attributed to the human. In addition, the identity of the human and of the defect evaluator is never stated, there is no blinding, and the Qwen check (Table 11) measures plans, not defects.

pattern_stance_changes.reason: The only execution evidence (Table 10) rests on an Auto-SPOQ baseline that contradicts Table 8. The human is unidentified (likely an author), the evaluator is unspecified, and there are 4 tasks with no blinding. Rework rises (1.00 to 2.50) and LOC churn rises (5.75 to 104.25), with no time or cost accounting for the human. This is not evidence that clears the 'supports' bar.

missed_issues: Factual error in the first review: it says 'No repository URL for SPOQ or benchmarks' and lists closed_artifacts. Line 73 gives 'Source code: https://gitlab.com/kenth56/spoq — reference implementation, epic definitions, validation skills, and all case study artifacts.' Reproducibility should be about 2, not 1, although the evaluator identity and defect-counting procedure are still not described in the paper.

COI is understated as medium. The authors evaluate their own named methodology with their own rubric on tasks they wrote. The 'External' Case Study 2 is Pinpoint, a B2B QA platform (Appendix B.4.2), which is the co-author's company (dheeraj@testwithpinpoint.com; 'Pinpoint Technologies LLC'). Four of the seven Table 12 projects are Pinpoint projects. Appendix B.7 carries an ROI pitch ('Director Model', '8x cost efficiency'). The rubric rule 'own product evaluated favorably without independent replication' points to high.

Table 9 (Qwen): the 'Overall' column equals the 'Defects' column exactly in all three rows (58.33/70.00/83.33), and the paper does not explain how it is aggregated. Under Full SPOQ, Rework (97.50 to 88.75) and LOC Churn (81.25 to 67.50) quality scores get worse. The claim of a 'preserved monotonic ordering' rests on that unexplained Overall score.

The abstract and §7 say 'direction and significance of the SPOQ gains are preserved', but no significance test appears anywhere, and §6.8 concedes the Qwen rows are single-shot. This is hype_language / unsupported.

Implausibly tight variances (e.g. Rework 1.00 ± 0.00, Warnings 0.00 ± 0.00, Coverage 99.75 ± 0.5) come from 4 runs per task over 4 author-written tasks with an unnamed evaluator, which raises self_reported_numbers concerns.

Field statistics: 7,907 of 8,589 commits (92%) come from one repo whose owner is thanked in the Acknowledgments for 'adoption ... and candid feedback'. The 99.87% pass rate covers agent-written tests (survivorship / metric_mismatch).
note: The first review found the key Table 8 vs Table 10 inconsistency and the Pinpoint 'external' issue, but it still admitted the paper. It also misstated that no code URL exists. Given the anomalous baselines, the unnamed evaluators, the claimed significance with no tests, and self-promotion by the authors' own company, the quantitative claims should not be load-bearing. At most, the Appendix B.5 failure catalogue is usable as anecdote.
